messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forester
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 52

He is 54, a married forester who has spent most of his adult life in the woods, trusting the rhythm of trees, weather, and equipment more than the uncertainty of people. Before the event that changed things, he describes himself as steady, practical, and not especially reflective. He was the kind of man who got up before dawn, packed his lunch in the same thermos each day, and measured seasons by the growth rings of timber and the sound of chainsaws in the distance.

The injury happened on an ordinary workday that now feels to him like the dividing line between two lives. He was supervising a logging operation, moving through familiar terrain with a crew he knew well. In a brief sequence of misjudgments, a routine task went wrong, and another worker was seriously injured. He can still picture the moment with painful precision: the angle of the body, the sound that followed, the sudden stillness after a burst of movement. He calls it an accident, but he also returns again and again to the split-second decisions he wishes he had made differently. Since then, his mind has not let him keep the event in the past. It replays in fragments, often when he least expects it—while driving, while sharpening tools, while hearing a metallic clang in the shop. The images arrive without invitation and carry the same force as the original moment.

In the immediate aftermath, he goes into a kind of shock that he initially mistakes for competence. He focuses on what needs to be done, speaks in a flat voice, and completes calls and reports because there is no other option. Later, when the practical demands ease, the emotional weight settles in. He begins to sleep badly, waking with his heart racing after vivid dreams that leave him disoriented and ashamed. Some nights he checks the locks, then checks them again, unable to convince himself that the house is secure. He lies awake replaying the day in reverse, looking for the point where things might have turned out differently. He is not simply afraid of what happened; he is haunted by what it means about him.

At work, he becomes increasingly cautious and tense. The forest, once a place of competence and belonging, now feels unpredictable. He notices every change in terrain, every snapped branch, every shift in a crew member’s tone. He jumps at sudden noise. A falling limb, a shouted warning, even the sharp whine of a saw can send a surge of panic through his chest and shoulders. He keeps his face controlled, but his body remains on alert as though another disaster is waiting just beyond the next stand of trees. He double-checks instructions, then checks them again, afraid that a moment’s distraction could lead to another irreversible mistake. The work he once relied on to steady him now leaves him drained.

He also withdraws from the people closest to him. His wife notices that he is quieter at dinner, slower to answer questions, and more likely to leave the room when conversations become emotionally charged. He wants to protect her from his guilt, but in doing so he becomes more isolated. He does not speak easily about the injured coworker, though he thinks of him often and wonders about his recovery. He feels responsible in a way that is hard to explain to anyone who was not there. That responsibility has hardened into self-reproach. He tells himself he should have seen it coming, should have intervened sooner, should have known better. Even when others call it a tragic accident, he struggles to hear anything except accusation.

He has begun to avoid the reminders that trigger the sharpest surge of distress. He takes different routes to work when he can. He postpones maintenance tasks that would bring him near the site where the injury happened. He limits time with work photos and equipment records. At the same time, he cannot fully escape the event; it follows him into quiet moments and intrudes in the middle of ordinary tasks. He notices that he is less able to enjoy things that used to matter, including weekend time in the woods with his family. He feels distant, narrowed, as if part of him remains frozen on that day.

Now, months later, he still functions outwardly, but with great effort. People who know him see a man who gets the job done. He knows how much energy it takes to keep himself composed, to prevent the memories from showing on his face, to push through the tightness in his chest and the constant sense that something terrible is still about to happen. The accident has not only changed the way he works; it has altered how he moves through the world, with caution, guilt, and an unrelenting sense that one mistake has become impossible to outgrow.
